description.context: When a NordGrid junior engineer wants to understand what Spark is actually doing with their code, they call df.explain() — a method that prints Spark's execution plan. There are two common ways to call it: df.explain() prints ONLY the physical plan (what Spark will run), and df.explain(True) prints all four phases (Parsed, Analyzed, Optimized, and Physical) so the engineer can see how Catalyst rewrote the query at each step. Junior engineers usually want only the physical plan because that is what runs.
description.task: Which output is from .explain() and which is from .explain(True)?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code Called First: meters.filter(col('daily_kw') > 100).explain()

Code Called Second: meters.filter(col('daily_kw') > 100).explain(True)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Two output samples from the same query — one called with .explain(), one with .explain(True)

fields.label: Which output is from .explain() and which is from .explain(True)?
options: A is .explain() — physical plan only. B is .explain(True) — all four phases including Parsed, Analyzed, Optimized, and Physical.
Both are .explain() output; the difference is that B was called on a more complex query that triggered more Catalyst rewrites and so produced more output.
A is .explain(True). B is .explain(). True turns OFF the verbose phase-by-phase output and prints only the compact physical-plan summary.
A is .explain(extended=False) and B is .explain(extended=True). The True/False parameter for explain() is named 'extended', not used positionally.
fields.correctAnswer: A is .explain() — physical plan only. B is .explain(True) — all four phases including Parsed, Analyzed, Optimized, and Physical.
fields.rationale: explain() with no argument.explain(True).The two are produced from the same query — the only difference is how much detail the engineer asked for.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Treats explain output as query-complexity-driven.Output structure depends on the explain mode, not query complexity.

tasks.title: Parsed vs Analyzed vs Optimized vs Physical

description.context: When .explain(True) prints all four phases, each phase represents a stage in Catalyst's optimization journey. The Parsed Logical Plan is what Spark first understood from your code (column names may show as unresolved). The Analyzed Logical Plan resolves column references against the actual schema (so column types appear). The Optimized Logical Plan is what Catalyst rewrote — adding pushdown predicates, removing dead columns, folding constants. The Physical Plan is what Spark will actually run, with concrete operators like FileScan, Filter, and Exchange.

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Code: meters.filter(col('region') == 'NORTH').select('meter_id').explain(True)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Four plan excerpts shuffled out of order; identify which is which phase

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
Excerpt W:
  Project [meter_id#0]
  +- Filter (isnotnull(region#5) AND (region#5 = NORTH))
     +- Relation [meter_id#0,region#5] parquet

Excerpt X:
  *(1) Project [meter_id#0]
  +- *(1) Filter (isnotnull(region#5) AND (region#5 = NORTH))
     +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
        +- FileScan parquet [meter_id#0,region#5] PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(region), EqualTo(region,NORTH)]

Excerpt Y:
  meter_id: string
  Project [meter_id#0]
  +- Filter (region#5 = NORTH)
     +- Relation [meter_id#0,region#5] parquet

Excerpt Z:
  'Project ['meter_id]
  +- 'Filter ('region = NORTH)
     +- 'UnresolvedRelation [meters]

fields.label: Which excerpt is which phase?
options: W=Parsed, X=Analyzed, Y=Optimized, Z=Physical. Order follows alphabetical letter assignment to phase order in the standard Spark printout.
All four are the same plan printed at different verbosity settings; quote marks and the # numbering change but the underlying tree structure is identical across all phases.
X=Parsed, W=Analyzed, Z=Optimized, Y=Physical. Excerpts go in reverse order from the printed output, so X (with FileScan) is actually the parsed phase.
Z is Parsed because UnresolvedRelation appears. Y is Analyzed because types appear. W is Optimized because IsNotNull was added. X is Physical because FileScan appears.
fields.correctAnswer: Z is Parsed because UnresolvedRelation appears. Y is Analyzed because types appear. W is Optimized because IsNotNull was added. X is Physical because FileScan appears.
fields.rationale: Z is Parsed: 'UnresolvedRelation' and quoted columns ('meter_id) mean Spark has not yet matched names to the schema.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Assigns phases by letter order; the actual mapping is identifiable from content markers.
Option B: Treats the four phases as the same plan.

tasks.title: FileScan, Filter, Project — The First Three

description.context: Three of the most common operators in any physical plan are FileScan, Filter, and Project. FileScan is the line that says 'read these columns from these files on disk'. Filter is the line that narrows ROWS — only those matching a condition pass through. Project is the line that narrows COLUMNS — only the listed columns continue. Physical plans read BOTTOM-TO-TOP: the bottom operator runs first, then its result flows up to the next operator. So a plan with FileScan at the bottom, Filter in the middle, and Project at the top means Spark scans first, filters next, projects last.
description.task: What does Spark do FIRST when running this plan?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Code: meters.filter(col('daily_kw') > 100).select('meter_id', 'daily_kw').explain()

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Minimal 4-line plan with FileScan, Filter, and Project — student labels each operator and confirms execution order

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Project [meter_id#0, daily_kw#3]
+- *(1) Filter (isnotnull(daily_kw#3) AND (daily_kw#3 > 100.0))
   +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
      +- FileScan parquet [meter_id#0,daily_kw#3] PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(daily_kw), GreaterThan(daily_kw,100.0)]

fields.label: What does Spark do FIRST when running this plan?
options: Project — Spark first chooses which columns to keep (meter_id, daily_kw). The Project line is at the top of the plan, and physical plans run top-to-bottom.
Filter — Spark first applies the filter condition daily_kw > 100. The filter is between Project and FileScan in the plan, and runs before either.
FileScan — Spark first reads the columns from the parquet files. FileScan is the bottom operator in the plan, and physical plans run bottom-to-top.
ColumnarToRow — Spark first converts columnar parquet format into row format because all subsequent operators need row-style data. ColumnarToRow runs before FileScan.
fields.correctAnswer: FileScan — Spark first reads the columns from the parquet files. FileScan is the bottom operator in the plan, and physical plans run bottom-to-top.
fields.rationale: Physical plans read bottom-to-top: the operator at the bottom runs first, and its output flows up.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Reads physical plans top-to-bottom; they execute bottom-to-top.
Option B: Picks the middle operator without applying the bottom-to-top rule.

description.context: Exchange is the operator name Spark uses for a SHUFFLE — moving rows between executors. When data needs to be redistributed (because a groupBy needs all rows with the same key on the same executor, or a join needs matching keys co-located), Spark inserts an Exchange operator in the plan. The most common form is Exchange hashpartitioning(column, N) — meaning Spark hashes that column and sends each row to one of N partitions. Other forms exist (Exchange RangePartitioning for sorts, Exchange RoundRobinPartitioning for balanced repartitioning) but hash partitioning is the one Junior engineers see most often.
description.task: What does the Exchange line tell you about what Spark is doing?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Code: meters.groupBy('region').agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total')).explain()

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Plan with one Exchange hashpartitioning operator visible from a groupBy

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- HashAggregate(keys=[region#5], functions=[sum(daily_kw#3)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region#5, 200), [plan_id=14]
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[region#5], functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw#3)])
         +- FileScan parquet [region#5,daily_kw#3]

fields.label: What does the Exchange line tell you about what Spark is doing?
options: Spark is sorting the data by region before aggregating; Exchange means a sort step takes place. The number 200 is how many sort buffers Spark will use.
Spark is shuffling by hashing region into 200 partitions; rows with the same region land on the same executor so HashAggregate above can sum them. Exchange means shuffle.
Exchange is an internal Spark operator that does not affect runtime; it is a placeholder Catalyst inserts during planning that disappears at execution time.
Spark is doing data exchange between the driver and executors; the 200 means 200 rows are sent at a time. This is how Spark transmits results to the application from worker nodes.
fields.correctAnswer: Spark is shuffling by hashing region into 200 partitions; rows with the same region land on the same executor so HashAggregate above can sum them. Exchange means shuffle.
fields.rationale: Exchange is the physical-plan name for a SHUFFLE — redistributing rows across executors.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Confuses Exchange with Sort.Exchange is movement; Sort is ordering.Different operators.

description.context: When you write a filter like .filter(col('daily_kw') > 100), you might expect Spark to load every row and then check the condition. It usually does something smarter: it tells the file reader to skip rows that fail the condition BEFORE they enter Spark's memory. This optimization is called PREDICATE PUSHDOWN. In a physical plan, look at the FileScan line for a field called PushedFilters: [...]. Filter conditions that pushed down appear in this list. Conditions that did NOT push down stay as a separate Filter operator above the FileScan. Pushdown matters because it can reduce data read from disk by 100× or more.
description.task: Which condition pushed down to the file reader, and which did not?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Code: meters.filter((col('daily_kw') > 100) & (col('region') == 'NORTH')).explain()

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: A physical plan from a NordGrid query with two filter conditions, one pushed down and one not

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(1) Filter (isnotnull(daily_kw#3) AND (daily_kw#3 > 100.0))
+- *(1) ColumnarToRow
   +- FileScan parquet [meter_id#0,daily_kw#3,region#5]
      PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(region), EqualTo(region,NORTH)]

fields.label: Which condition pushed down to the file reader, and which did not?
options: Both conditions pushed down. The Filter operator above is a leftover that Spark always shows even when filters are fully pushed down to the file reader; safe to ignore.
Neither condition pushed down. PushedFilters: [...] is just a debug label; actual filtering always happens in the Filter operator above the FileScan line.
region == 'NORTH' pushed down (it is in PushedFilters). daily_kw > 100 did NOT push down (it remained as a separate Filter above FileScan). Both happen but at different layers.
daily_kw > 100 pushed down because it is in the Filter operator at the top of the plan. region == 'NORTH' did not push down because it appears below FileScan in the PushedFilters list.
fields.correctAnswer: region == 'NORTH' pushed down (it is in PushedFilters). daily_kw > 100 did NOT push down (it remained as a separate Filter above FileScan). Both happen but at different layers.
fields.rationale: PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(region), EqualTo(region,NORTH)] tells you which conditions the parquet reader applied while loading.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats the residual Filter operator as inert; it is the actual second-stage filter.
Option B: Treats PushedFilters as decorative.

tasks.title: Why a UDF Filter Did Not Push Down

description.context: Not every filter can push down. For pushdown to work, Spark needs to express the condition in a form the file reader understands — equality, range comparison, IS NULL, IS NOT NULL, simple boolean combinations. When you wrap a column in a Python UDF (a user-defined function), Spark cannot translate the function call into something the file reader can evaluate. The file reader is a Java/native library; it does not run Python code. So filters using UDFs always stay as a separate Filter operator above the FileScan, and Spark must load every row to evaluate them.
description.task: Why does Plan B's filter not push down, and what is the runtime cost?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code A: meters.filter(col('daily_kw') > 100).explain()

Code B: is_high = udf(lambda kw: kw > 100, 'boolean')
meters.filter(is_high(col('daily_kw'))).explain()

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Two side-by-side plans from queries that look similar — one filter pushes down, one does not because of a UDF

fields.label: Why does Plan B's filter not push down, and what is the runtime cost?
options: Plan B uses a UDF; Spark cannot translate Python code into a parquet reader predicate. PushedFilters is empty, so the reader returns ALL rows. BatchEvalPython runs the UDF in a Python worker. Cost: full scan plus Python overhead.
Plan B's UDF correctly pushed down — BatchEvalPython is the optimized form of pushdown for Python functions. The empty PushedFilters list is misleading; Spark uses a different mechanism for UDFs.
Plan B's filter pushes down but produces wrong results because the UDF returns Python bool instead of Java Boolean; the cast in BatchEvalPython is a workaround. Cost: small CPU overhead for the cast.
Plan B is functionally identical to Plan A. BatchEvalPython is added by Catalyst even when no Python is involved; PushedFilters is empty because of an unrelated planner bug. Cost: same as Plan A.
fields.correctAnswer: Plan B uses a UDF; Spark cannot translate Python code into a parquet reader predicate. PushedFilters is empty, so the reader returns ALL rows. BatchEvalPython runs the UDF in a Python worker. Cost: full scan plus Python overhead.
fields.rationale: PushedFilters: [] in Plan B is the key signal.The parquet reader applies no filter and returns all rows.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Misreads BatchEvalPython as pushdown.It is UDF evaluation AFTER the file is read.
Option C: Invents a casting bug.

description.context: Every groupBy plan in Spark contains TWO HashAggregate operators, not one. The bottom one — labeled HashAggregate(...partial_sum...) — runs on each executor BEFORE the shuffle. It does a local reduction so each executor only sends its already-summed rows over the network. The top one — labeled HashAggregate(...sum...) — runs AFTER the Exchange and combines the partial results from all executors into the final answer. This pattern is called the COMBINER PATTERN. The partial step dramatically reduces shuffle volume: a 12M-row groupBy with 4 regions sends 4 partial rows per executor instead of millions of raw rows.
description.task: Why does the plan have TWO HashAggregate operators?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Code: meters.groupBy('region').agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total')).explain()

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: A groupBy plan showing the partial+final HashAggregate pattern with Exchange between them

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- HashAggregate(keys=[region#5], functions=[sum(daily_kw#3)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region#5, 200), [plan_id=14]
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[region#5], functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw#3)])
         +- FileScan parquet [region#5,daily_kw#3]

fields.label: Why does the plan have TWO HashAggregate operators?
options: Spark made a mistake; one of the HashAggregate operators is redundant in this plan. The optimizer should have removed it but did not. Performance impact: minor double-work that runs twice.
The bottom one (partial_sum) is incomplete and produces wrong results; the top one (sum) re-runs the aggregation correctly. Spark always retries aggregations to ensure correctness.

The bottom HashAggregate(partial_sum) reduces rows on each executor BEFORE the shuffle, so only summed-per-executor rows cross the network. The top HashAggregate combines the partials. This is the combiner pattern.
The two HashAggregate operators handle different parts of the GROUP BY clause; the bottom handles the keys, the top handles the aggregate function. They are independent steps, not related.
fields.correctAnswer: The bottom HashAggregate(partial_sum) reduces rows on each executor BEFORE the shuffle, so only summed-per-executor rows cross the network. The top HashAggregate combines the partials. This is the combiner pattern.
fields.rationale: The combiner pattern is one of the most important reading skills for groupBy plans.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats the partial as redundant; it is the optimizer's correct optimization.

tasks.title: The Plan Without a Partial Stage

description.context: The partial+final HashAggregate pattern only works when the aggregate function can be split into a partial step and a final step. Built-in aggregates like sum, count, min, max, avg can be split — they are MERGEABLE. But certain user-defined aggregates and some functions like collect_list cannot be split because their accumulator state cannot be merged across partitions. When that happens, Catalyst skips the partial step and produces a plan with only ONE HashAggregate above the Exchange. Every row of input must then shuffle before aggregation. At 12M rows the difference is dramatic.
description.task: What is the key difference between the two plans, and what is the performance impact?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code A: meters.groupBy('region').agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total')).explain()

Code B: meters.groupBy('region').agg(collect_list('meter_id').alias('ids')).explain()

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Two side-by-side plans for similar groupBy queries — one with partial+final, one with only final

fields.label: What is the key difference between the two plans, and what is the performance impact?
options: Plan B uses ObjectHashAggregate instead of HashAggregate; this is a naming variant for the same operation. No performance difference between the two plans.
Plan B is faster because it has fewer operators; fewer steps means less coordination overhead. Plan A has redundant HashAggregate operators that slow it down considerably.
Plan A has a missing operator — there should be a Sort step before aggregation; this is a Catalyst bug. Plan B is the correctly-optimized form of the query.
Plan A has TWO HashAggregate stages (partial+final). Plan B has only ONE because collect_list cannot split across partitions. Plan B shuffles every input row; Plan A shuffles only summed rows.
fields.correctAnswer: Plan A has TWO HashAggregate stages (partial+final). Plan B has only ONE because collect_list cannot split across partitions. Plan B shuffles every input row; Plan A shuffles only summed rows.
fields.rationale: Plan A has the partial+final pattern with a partial_sum step BEFORE the Exchange, so each executor reduces its local data before shuffling.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats ObjectHashAggregate vs HashAggregate as the difference; the missing partial step matters more.

description.context: Time to put it all together. A NordGrid junior engineer wrote a query that joins meter readings with substation reference data and aggregates by region. The senior engineer asks them to read the resulting physical plan and answer four questions about it. Every operator from PRJ2 should be recognizable; the partial+final pattern from PRJ4 should appear; and one new feature shows up for the first time — the BroadcastHashJoin operator, which is what Spark uses when one side of a join is small enough to copy to every executor.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: A 4-stage physical plan from a meters × substations join with groupBy aggregation

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
code = (meters
    .filter(col('daily_kw') > 100)
    .join(broadcast(substations), on='substation_id', how='inner')
    .groupBy('region')
    .agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total_kw'), count('*').alias('n_meters')))
code.explain()

== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- HashAggregate(keys=[region#22], functions=[sum(daily_kw#3), count(1)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region#22, 200), [plan_id=58]
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[region#22], functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw#3), partial_count(1)])
         +- Project [daily_kw#3, region#22]
            +- BroadcastHashJoin [substation_id#7], [substation_id#19], Inner, BuildRight
               :- Filter (isnotnull(daily_kw#3) AND (daily_kw#3 > 100.0))
               :  +- ColumnarToRow
               :     +- FileScan parquet [meter_id#0, daily_kw#3, substation_id#7]
               :        PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(daily_kw), GreaterThan(daily_kw,100.0), IsNotNull(substation_id)]
               +- BroadcastExchange HashedRelationBroadcastMode
                  +- Filter isnotnull(substation_id#19)
                     +- FileScan parquet [substation_id#19, region#22]
                        PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(substation_id)]

description.context: Final exercise of the Junior track. The same NordGrid query is run twice — once without a broadcast hint and once with broadcast(substations). The two plans look different. The student is asked to compare them and answer four questions about WHAT differs, WHY one is faster, where AQE annotations show up at runtime, and what would change at 100× scale. Every operator from PRJ2-PRJ4 is in play, plus the AdaptiveSparkPlan annotation that shows up in modern Spark.

evidence.content: Two physical plans for the same query — Plan A without broadcast hint, Plan B with broadcast hint

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
# Plan A — no broadcast hint
code_a = (meters
    .join(substations, on='substation_id', how='inner')
    .groupBy('region').agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total')))
code_a.explain()

         +- Project [daily_kw#3, region#22]
            +- SortMergeJoin [substation_id#7], [substation_id#19], Inner
               :- Sort [substation_id#7 ASC NULLS FIRST], false
               :  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(substation_id#7, 200)
               :     +- FileScan parquet meters
               +- Sort [substation_id#19 ASC NULLS FIRST], false
                  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(substation_id#19, 200)
                     +- FileScan parquet substations

    .join(broadcast(substations), on='substation_id', how='inner')
    .groupBy('region').agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total')))
code_b.explain()

== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- HashAggregate(keys=[region#22], functions=[sum(daily_kw#3)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region#22, 200)
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[region#22], functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw#3)])
         +- Project [daily_kw#3, region#22]
            +- BroadcastHashJoin [substation_id#7], [substation_id#19], Inner, BuildRight
               :- FileScan parquet meters
               +- BroadcastExchange HashedRelationBroadcastMode
                  +- FileScan parquet substations
